title: Signal Flips
statement: Two relay switches each store a non-negative integer as 31 binary toggles. To turn the pattern of a into the pattern of b, a technician flips toggles one at a time. Return how many toggles must be flipped, which is the number of bit positions where a and b differ.

examples.explanation: 1 is 001 and 4 is 100; they differ in two positions.

hints.content: Look at the two numbers in binary, position by position.
XOR produces 1 exactly where two bits differ.
So the answer is the number of 1 bits in a ^ b.
You can count 1 bits by testing x & 1 and shifting right, one position at a time.
Faster: x &= x - 1 clears the lowest 1 bit, so count how many times you can do that before x becomes 0.

testCases.explanation: 1 is 001 and 4 is 100; they differ in two positions.
Every one of the 31 toggles differs.
The highest and lowest positions differ.
All ones versus alternating bits: 15 flips.

solutions.title: Compare binary strings
solutions.intuition: Write both numbers as 31-digit binary strings and count positions that differ.
solutions.approach: Use toString(2) and padStart(31, '0') on both, then compare characters.
solutions.pseudocode: sa = binary(a, 31 digits); sb = binary(b, 31 digits); return count of i with sa[i] != sb[i]
commonMistakes: Forgetting to pad, which misaligns numbers of different lengths.
Comparing the strings from the left without padding, which compares the wrong positions.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Working with padded binary strings mirrors the definition. It's constant time for 31 bits but allocates strings.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: They differ at the 1s place and the 4s place: 2 flips.

solutions.title: Popcount of XOR
solutions.intuition: XOR marks every differing position with a 1 bit.
solutions.approach: Compute x = a ^ b and repeatedly clear its lowest set bit with x &= x - 1, counting iterations.
solutions.pseudocode: x = a xor b; count = 0; while x != 0: x = x and (x - 1); count++; return count
commonMistakes: Using >> on values with the sign bit set; here inputs stay below 2^31, so a ^ b is never negative.
Writing x & x - 1 without parentheses in languages where precedence differs.
solutions.interviewExplanation: XOR leaves a 1 wherever the bits differ, so the answer is the popcount of a ^ b. Clearing the lowest set bit with x & (x - 1) runs once per set bit. Many languages also expose popcount as a built-in.
